summary: Describes how SIP is used for subscriptions and notifications about presence, meaning a person's willingness and ability to communicate. It goes beyond simple online and offline flags to support richer status information.

plainLanguage.summary: It is how a chat app shows that a friend is available, busy or away. This document explains how the app asks for and gets those updates.

questions: how does sip subscribe and notify work
subtitle: How SIP lets one party subscribe to another's presence and get notified when it changes.

tldr.problem: Instant messaging and communication systems need a way to tell others whether a user is willing and able to communicate, which is richer than a simple on-line or off-line flag.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a SIP event package named presence. A watcher sends SUBSCRIBE to a presence agent, which authenticates and authorizes it, then sends NOTIFY messages carrying presence documents.
tldr.outcome: SIP networks can be reused for presence subscriptions and notifications, and the package is compliant with the Common Presence Profile (CPP). The RFC is a Proposed Standard.

facts.label: Notification rate
facts.value: No more than once every five seconds per presentity (SHOULD NOT exceed)

today: RFC 3856 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 8996. It has not been obsoleted. It depends on RFC 3261 and RFC 3265.

sections.title: Presence over SIP
sections.content:
Presence conveys the ability and willingness of a user to communicate across a set of devices. RFC 2778 models a presence service as a system that accepts, stores and distributes presence information to interested parties called watchers. This RFC proposes using the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) as the presence protocol.

It does so by defining an event package within the SIP event notification framework of RFC 3265, using its SUBSCRIBE and NOTIFY methods. The RFC argues that SIP suits this because SIP location services already hold presence information in the form of registrations. SIP networks can also route requests from any user to the server holding a user's registration state, so SUBSCRIBE requests can reach it too.

The package rests on a new logical entity, the presence agent (PA), which accepts subscriptions, stores their state and generates notifications when presence changes. It is also compliant with the Common Presence Profile (CPP), which helps SIP interwork with other CPP systems.
sections.plainLanguage: Many chat tools can already tell who is around. This document teaches one messaging system, SIP, to share that news in a standard way.

sections.title: Who Does What
sections.content:
The RFC defines several roles. A Presence User Agent (PUA) manipulates presence information for a presentity, for example by sending a REGISTER request or by publishing a presence document. A presentity can have many PUAs, such as a cell phone and a PDA. PUAs push data into the system but do not receive SUBSCRIBE or send NOTIFY. A Presence Agent receives SUBSCRIBE requests and generates notifications. A presence server is a physical entity that can act as a PA or proxy SUBSCRIBE requests. An edge presence server is a PA co-located with a PUA.

The flow is simple. A subscriber sends SUBSCRIBE naming the presentity in the Request-URI. The PA authenticates it, then authorizes it. A 200 OK means authorized, and a 202 means the subscription is pending. In both cases the PA sends an immediate NOTIFY with the state of the presentity and of the subscription. After that it sends a NOTIFY for each change. The subscription creates a SIP dialog, and the subscriber must refresh it before it expires. Sending SUBSCRIBE with an Expires value of zero ends it. Doing so also works as a one-time fetch of the current state.
sections.plainLanguage: You ask a helper to watch your friend's status. The helper checks that your friend allows it, then tells you right away and again whenever the status changes.

sections.title: Presence URIs
sections.content:
A presentity can be named with a SIP or SIPS URI, or with the protocol-independent pres URI, of the form pres:user@domain. A pres URI is resolved to a protocol-specific URI through domain mapping policies on a server.

If a subscriber knows both a valid pres URI and a SIP URI for a presentity, it SHOULD use the pres URI. The same goes for the From and To header fields. The reason is interoperability: a protocol-independent name can pass through gateways to other CPP systems, whereas gateways would otherwise have to map SIP URIs into foreign formats, which has known problems. The rule is a SHOULD, not a MUST, because proxies that do not understand the pres scheme will reject the request, and the RFC expects many systems to start out giving users only a SIP URI.

Where one URI is learned from another, for instance a SIP URI learned from the Contact header of a 200 OK to a pres SUBSCRIBE, lookup services SHOULD have some kind of scoping mechanism (RECOMMENDED), such as a DNS TTL, so stale URIs can be detected.
sections.plainLanguage: The pres address is like a person's name, and the SIP address is like their street address. Using the name works everywhere the name is understood.

sections.title: The Presence Event Package
sections.content:
The package name is presence, carried in the Event header field of SUBSCRIBE and NOTIFY. It defines no extra event parameters. IANA registration lists it as a package, with RFC 3856 as the published document.

A SUBSCRIBE normally has no body, because the Request-URI plus the package name is enough. A body may carry a filter document that limits which events trigger notifications or what data comes back. Filter documents are not specified here and were expected to be the subject of future standardization. Honouring them is at the PA's discretion.

The default subscription duration is 3600 seconds, reflecting that presence changes (turning a phone on or off, changing registration, changing status in an instant messaging tool) occur on the order of seconds to hours. A subscriber MAY ask for another value in the Expires header field.

NOTIFY bodies carry a presence document. All subscribers and notifiers MUST support application/pidf+xml, which is also the default when SUBSCRIBE has no Accept header. If Accept is present it MUST include that type and MAY list others.
sections.plainLanguage: The subscription is a sign-up for status updates that lasts about an hour unless you ask for a different time. Updates arrive in one agreed note format.

sections.title: Authentication and Authorization
sections.content:
Presence is highly sensitive, so the PA MUST authenticate every subscription request using any mechanism from RFC 3261. Digest is mandatory to implement. For single-domain systems, digest over TLS is suggested. Between domains, identity may rest on transitive trust and network asserted identity. SIPS URIs and S/MIME are also options.

After authentication the PA decides on authorization, and it MUST NOT accept a subscription unless the presentity has authorized it. How is out of scope; it could be access lists, an uploaded document or a back-end authorization server. The RFC reduces every decision to three states:

  • Successful: answered with 200.
  • Rejected: answered with 403 or 603.
  • Pending: answered with 202, used when authorization cannot yet be obtained.

For a pending subscription, the presentity state SHOULD include a textual note that shows the pending status. A PA can also do polite blocking: it answers 200 OK even to a rejected or pending subscription, then sends a NOTIFY that does not reveal the block, typically showing off-line status for a single contact address.
sections.plainLanguage: The helper first checks who you are, then checks that your friend said yes. If your friend has not answered or said no, you might be told "away" so nobody feels singled out.

sections.title: Sending and Receiving Notifications
sections.content:
A PA MAY send a NOTIFY at any time, usually when the presentity's state changes. A reasonable baseline policy is to send one when any presence tuple changes, containing the complete current state. The body MUST use a type listed in the latest SUBSCRIBE Accept header, or application/pidf+xml if none was given. After a pending subscription is decided, a NOTIFY SHOULD follow for success and MAY follow for rejection. A PA SHOULD NOT generate notifications for one presentity more often than once every five seconds.

Each NOTIFY holds either no presence document or the complete, coherent state. Within a dialog, the document in the NOTIFY with the highest CSeq is current. If it has none, the one with the next highest CSeq is used. Notifications may be encrypted or signed with S/MIME. Signatures SHOULD come from an authority over the presentity's domain.

Forked SUBSCRIBE requests may create only a single dialog. A presentity can have several PAs, but they should be homogeneous. If aggregation is needed, it MUST be done by a PA representing the presentity.
sections.plainLanguage: Updates go out when something changes, but not too often. Each update is a full picture, and the newest one wins.

sections.title: State Agents and Learning Presence
sections.content:
When the PA is not co-located with the PUA, it acts as a state agent. It collects state from the PUAs and aggregates it into one presence document. The RFC says state agents are fundamental to presence, and that they are what a presence server is. One way for a state agent to get state is to subscribe to each PUA. Then PUAs SHOULD be able to act as PAs and accept authenticated subscriptions from the presentity's domain. State agents SHOULD support the watcherinfo template-package, so a user can be asked for an authorization decision.

A PA MAY migrate subscriptions to a PUA, for example to reduce state in the network. A PUA can hint at support by using the callee capabilities mechanism in REGISTER. If a migration fails with 405 or 489, the server acts as PA itself and SHOULD NOT retry for that registration. A PA SHOULD NOT migrate while it aggregates documents from several PUAs.

Section 7 lists informational ways a PA can learn presence: co-location with the PUA, registrations (where REGISTER requests used this way MUST be authenticated), and uploading presence documents, which is RECOMMENDED when a PUA wants direct control of what subscribers see.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone has a phone and a tablet, a central helper gathers news from both into one status. Sometimes the helper hands the job to the device itself.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC calls presence highly sensitive and covers several threats. For confidentiality, it combines hop-by-hop encryption (TLS RECOMMENDED between elements) with optional end-to-end S/MIME. Hop-by-hop reveals content to proxies; end-to-end does not hide everything and is open to traffic analysis. For integrity and authenticity, forged NOTIFY documents could fool a watcher, so watchers MUST support HTTP Digest, and PAs MUST support TLS and SIPS as if they were proxies.

For replay prevention, a stale off-line document could be replayed to block communication. When S/MIME is used for this, the document MUST carry a timestamp, and older tuples SHOULD be treated as stale. Digest with auth-int can also help.

For denial of service, presence has amplification: one SUBSCRIBE can cause a long stream of notifications, and an attacker can put a victim's address in Contact. RFC 3265 counters this by removing a subscription whose NOTIFY is unacknowledged or unwanted. Authorization policy that refuses unknown watchers helps, and servers can use digest, source address checks and 503 back-off.
sections.plainLanguage: Because status is private, every message is checked and can be locked. The rules also stop someone from tricking a helper into flooding a stranger with updates.

items.label: Successful
items.desc: The watcher may learn some subset of presence state.

items.label: Rejected
items.desc: The watcher will never receive any presence state.

items.label: Pending
items.desc: Not yet known whether the subscription is successful or rejected.
